title: Variolation expertise across Ottoman, African and British networks
summary: Documented channels expose non-European and non-elite expertise, while leaving uptake denominators and origins uncertain.

stages.invention: Not established; older origin traditions are disputed.
stages.feasibility: Contemporary reports describe induced infection and subsequent protection, with selection and follow-up limitations.
stages.deployment: Reported Ottoman and African use; specified British and colonial encounters.
stages.diffusion: Qualitative correspondence and institutional discussion; no population diffusion curve.

counterevidence: Prior local dissemination and epidemic timing could explain uptake independently of elite brokers; surviving reports are selective.

episode.technology_configuration: Variolation using infectious smallpox material, distinct from later vaccination; methods were heterogeneous.
episode.task: Reduce risk of later natural smallpox, while incurring an immediate intervention risk.
episode.population: Practitioners, recipient families and named informants in surviving reports; not representative Ottoman/African/British populations.
episode.interval: c. 1700–1723, with older histories treated as retrospective context.
episode.adoption_measure: Qualitative reports of use and knowledge transfer; numerator and eligible-population denominator unavailable.
episode.observation_limits: Elite and colonial mediation; informant motives and precise identities cannot be fully reconstructed; no valid common risk ratio.

actors.chooser: Parents, practitioners and patrons in documented encounters; children were frequently not the decision-makers.
actors.payer: Family or patron payments appear in reports; systematic cost evidence absent.
actors.operator_maintainer: Experienced local practitioners including women; household aftercare not quantified.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Children and dependent people subjected to others' choices; potential contacts were not enumerated.
actors.ability_to_refuse: No representative consent record. Onesimus's enslavement constrains interpreting testimony as an autonomous market transaction; household authority over children is evident, adult refusal rates unknown.

labour.tasks: Hands-on inoculation and knowledge brokerage; some healers were remunerated, unpaid care unmeasured.
labour.entry_barriers: Experiential skill and trusted access; formal entry requirements varied and are not established here.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Elite writers controlled much surviving attribution; practitioner bargaining power and earnings unknown.
labour.transition: No individual employment-transition series; persistence of practice inferred only from reports.
labour.distribution: Knowledge contributors span gender/status groups; no income gains established.
labour.evidence_limit: Cannot estimate occupational growth, remuneration or changes in caregivers' total workload.

title: Ottoman vaccination law and uneven delivery
summary: Free provision and legitimacy efforts coexisted with compulsion and supply constraints; mandates are not coverage.

stages.deployment: 1840–1846 free-provision, instructional and legitimacy projects; observed institutional provision separated from promises.
stages.diffusion: Regulatory expansion in 1885, 1894, 1903 and 1915; actual coverage remained incomplete.
stages.scaling: Training, production and registration were attempted complements; comprehensive delivery not demonstrated.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Institutional populations more reachable than dispersed rural households; no comparable rates.

mechanisms: zero monetary price with residual access costs
counterevidence: Refusal, war and instability also mattered; official accounts cannot rank them against supply problems.

episode.technology_configuration: Smallpox vaccination organized through imperial medical institutions, local officials, supplies and certification.
episode.task: Protect subjects and populations; also expand official responsibility and knowledge of residents.
episode.population: Institutional groups named in law versus rural/general populations; their denominators are not reconstructed.
episode.adoption_measure: Legal eligibility/obligation and qualitative delivery history, not achieved coverage percentages.
episode.observation_limits: Regulations are normative; enforcement, successful takes and complete population denominators are missing.

actors.chooser: Sultan, ministries and local officials set rules; medical staff administered; families acted within those conditions.
actors.payer: Imperial/local funding intended; recipients entitled to free provision, but non-price costs not measured.
actors.operator_maintainer: Physicians, trained vaccinators, local clerics/leaders, registration personnel; household transport and return visits.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Children, migrants, students and workers whose access to institutions could depend on certification.
actors.ability_to_refuse: 1885 school/service conditions and later fines/obligations documented. Actual enforcement and rural ability to evade unknown; compliance does not establish consent.

labour.tasks: Training, vaccination, inspection, records and local mobilization; household attendance required unpaid time.
labour.entry_barriers: Literacy and professional certification requirements appear in policy; rural personnel shortages documented.
labour.bargaining_ownership: State certification and salaries shaped recognized practice; livelihood effects on older practitioners not quantified.
labour.transition: Decades-long institutional expansion documented; no worker cohort or wage panel.
labour.distribution: Institutional versus rural delivery contrast; no reliable class/gender earnings distribution.
labour.evidence_limit: Official workforce proposals cannot be counted as jobs actually filled or sustained.

title: Antiseptic surgery as a changing clinical practice
summary: Clinical demonstrations, changing protocols and disputed comparisons complicate a simple discovery-to-acceptance narrative.

stages.invention: No unique-inventor claim; earlier clinical and cleanliness traditions remain relevant.
stages.feasibility: Lister's cases and procedures support particular clinical observations, not an invariant protocol.
stages.deployment: Use by Lister and other surgeons with varying combinations and adaptations.
stages.diffusion: Professional demonstrations, publications and trainees; qualitative, not a surgeon-level diffusion rate.
stages.displacement/reversal: Selective adoption and modification undermine a clean antisepsis-to-asepsis sequence.

counterevidence: Epidemic cycles, case selection and general improvements complicate outcome attribution; status or material access may also shape adoption.

episode.technology_configuration: Evolving carbolic-based wound management, dressings and operative routines rather than a single chemical purchase.
episode.task: Reduce wound complications and expand feasible surgery.
episode.population: Specified surgeons/wards and published case groups; no representative British surgeon sample.
episode.interval: 1867–1890 debate; Lister's earlier treated cases are background to published claims.
episode.adoption_measure: Published case reports, small before/after series and documented teaching/adaptation; no general adoption denominator.
episode.observation_limits: Clinical selection, changing case mix and routines, historical reinterpretation and non-independent source reuse.

actors.chooser: Surgeons and hospital leadership selected methods; patients' influence varied and is not systematically documented.
actors.payer: Hospitals, practitioners and patients through varied arrangements; comparative treatment costs not measured.
actors.operator_maintainer: Surgeons, assistants, dressers and caregivers performed procedures and aftercare.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Patients exposed to choices and execution quality; nursing/dressing labour often not foregrounded.
actors.ability_to_refuse: One case narrative notes patient reluctance; no broad consent or refusal series. Treatment alternatives constrained by local hospital practice.

labour.tasks: More attention to dressings, materials, handling and repeatable routines; demonstration and teaching.
labour.entry_barriers: Hands-on skills and access to teaching/equipment; social/professional barriers not quantified.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Professional authority shaped accepted evidence and practice; worker bargaining and ownership not measured.
labour.transition: Practice changed across decades; no measured displacement of occupations or wage effect.
labour.distribution: Patient outcomes vary by procedure/ward; no credible occupational distribution estimates.
labour.evidence_limit: Cannot convert a skills transition into a net employment or income claim.

title: Municipal safe water and sewerage with contested mortality attribution
summary: A Massachusetts regional design supports local water/sewer complementarity; broader city-panel contributions remain disputed.

stages.deployment: Regional water/sewer completion and major-city filtration/chlorination installations are distinct episodes.
stages.diffusion: Dated municipal installations; dates need not equal universal household service.
stages.scaling: Regional finance and engineering connected multiple jurisdictions.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Some cities used different source-water configurations; the regional untreated and single-treatment municipalities serve as comparisons.

counterevidence: Other sanitary change, nutrition and population composition compete with health attribution; panel disagreements share records.

episode.technology_configuration: A: protected piped water plus regional sewerage around Boston. B: filtration/chlorination and other interventions in a major-city panel; coefficients not pooled.
episode.task: Supply usable water and remove sewage; protect health and address nuisance.
episode.population: A: 60 Massachusetts municipalities excluding Boston in estimation, including 15 receiving both treatments. B: 25 major cities, 1900–1940.
episode.adoption_measure: Municipal completion indicators and annual mortality; water/sewer interaction. Household connection/use not directly observed; city-panel rates use differing population denominators.
episode.observation_limits: Service dates, partial years, spillovers, population changes and cause-of-death coding; A and B have different populations and treatment configurations.

actors.chooser: Municipal and state authorities, engineering/health boards; household choices constrained by networks.
actors.payer: Regional/municipal public financing; Massachusetts law compelled participation and payment in the sewerage district.
actors.operator_maintainer: Engineers, construction and operating crews, inspectors; household connection work not fully measured.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Downstream communities, children and residents unable to choose the network or pollution source.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Jurisdictions within the mandated district could not simply opt out; household connection obligations/refusal rates not audited.

labour.tasks: Construction, pumping, treatment, maintenance, monitoring and records; occupational counts unavailable.
labour.entry_barriers: Capital, engineering skill, land/network rights and public authorization.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Public regional institutions controlled system choice; distribution of contracts, labour gains and ownership rents unexamined.
labour.transition: Infrastructure phased across decades; no individual labour transition data.
labour.distribution: Child mortality examined, including demographic heterogeneity; these are health outcomes, not wage or job distribution.
labour.evidence_limit: Cannot infer equitable livelihood gains from aggregate mortality reduction.

title: Penicillin from research material to industrial supply
summary: Production complements and coordination help explain the gap between a promising drug and usable supply.

stages.feasibility: Clinical promise and stable material were antecedents; this case concerns industrial reproducibility.
stages.deployment: Laboratory-to-company process transfer and plant investment.
stages.scaling: Media, strain, tank, extraction and sterile finishing improvements enabled much larger supply.
stages.diffusion: Clinical population coverage and allocation not quantified here.

counterevidence: Commemorative sources may overstate own institutions; counterfactual production routes and procurement effects remain unresolved.

episode.technology_configuration: Specified US fermentation and downstream-processing route linked to British penicillin research.
episode.task: Produce usable quantities for wartime treatment.
episode.population: NRRL collaborators and participating manufacturers, with Pfizer process detail; not all producers or recipients.
contemporary_alternatives: Other antibacterial treatments, with clinical substitutability not assessed
Potential alternative industrial routes not evaluated
episode.adoption_measure: Qualitative process and plant scaling; no verified common production series or treatment-population denominator.
episode.observation_limits: Company/public-laboratory retrospectives; no batch logs, primary contracts or allocation dataset inspected.

actors.chooser: Research teams, government coordinators and company management chose process and capital commitments.
actors.payer: Public research resources and company investment; exact procurement guarantees and shares unknown.
actors.operator_maintainer: Microbiologists, chemical engineers, plant operators and sterile-processing workers.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Patients facing scarce supply and workers whose capacity was diverted from other products.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Firms made investments under wartime pressures; precise contracting autonomy unknown. Patients could not choose unavailable supply.

labour.tasks: Culture development, fermentation control, extraction, purification and sterile finishing; transfer of existing industrial expertise.
labour.entry_barriers: Laboratories, capital, technical skill and controlled production environments.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Firm/state authority over production; patents, wage bargaining and distribution of returns not audited.
labour.transition: Rapid wartime scaling within several years; individual retraining and displacement unknown.
labour.distribution: Scarce supply and Allied wartime priorities visible, but recipient-class or worker outcomes unquantified.
labour.evidence_limit: No evidence-based net job count, wage effect or equitable-access estimate.

title: Sri Lankan malaria suppression, resurgence and elimination
summary: Successful suppression reversed when a maintained system weakened; later elimination combined continuing institutional functions.

stages.deployment: Postwar indoor residual spraying within the Anti-Malaria Campaign.
stages.scaling: Suppression reached very low recorded local transmission by 1963.
stages.displacement/reversal: 1964 relaxation followed by late-1960s resurgence; later resistance prompted insecticide replacement.
stages.diffusion: Coverage cannot be recovered directly from infection counts.
stages.feasibility: 2016 certification records sustained interrupted local transmission, not permanent absence of risk.

counterevidence: Detection intensity, migration, ecological change and resistance interact; retrospective labels such as complacency are not independently observed motives.

episode.technology_configuration: A: DDT indoor residual spraying, case detection and treatment. B: later adapted vector-control and surveillance system culminating in certification.
episode.task: Suppress and ultimately interrupt local malaria transmission.
episode.population: National reported cases with specific local observations; later certification population is Sri Lanka, imported infections distinct.
episode.interval: A 1945–1977 suppression/reversal/replacement; B later programme culminating in 2016.
episode.adoption_measure: Reported indigenous/imported cases, programme chronology and certification; not a population adoption rate.
episode.observation_limits: Changing surveillance, overlapping retrospective source traditions and absent district-level exposure denominator.

actors.chooser: Health ministry/Anti-Malaria Campaign and regional teams; donors and households also affected deployment.
actors.payer: Public health budgets with international support; complete finance series not inspected.
actors.operator_maintainer: Spray workers, diagnostic staff, clinicians, surveillance teams and participating households.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Residents exposed to others' infections, spray policies, land-use change and service disruption.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Household spray acceptance could vary; detailed refusal rights and enforcement not audited. Conflict and movement constrained practical access.

labour.tasks: Repeated spraying, microscopy/diagnosis, surveillance, treatment and coordinated field response.
labour.entry_barriers: Technical training, stable employment funding, transport and supplies; exact credential requirements unexamined.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Public programme and donor resource control; household voice and worker bargaining not measured.
labour.transition: Spraying teams were disbanded during relaxation; individual livelihood trajectories absent.
labour.distribution: Health exposure differed geographically, including conflict regions; no occupational income distribution measured.
labour.evidence_limit: Service capacity and staff counts are not evidence of net lifetime employment gains.

title: Oral rehydration research and household delivery in Bangladesh
region: Calcutta and India–Bangladesh border refugee camps
summary: Operational evidence and household teaching mattered, but competence, product availability and use were distinct; an uptake denominator discrepancy is preserved.

stages.feasibility: Late-1960s practical trials and 1971 caregiver-administered camp treatment reported in historical scholarship.
stages.deployment: Household teaching and ORS distribution through several organizations.
stages.scaling: BRAC's 1980s national-scale teaching campaign; reach is not successful use.
stages.diffusion: 1993 sample provides episode-based use measures and preparation tests.
stages.displacement/reversal: Packaged ORS grew alongside continued home preparation; no claim that home use disappeared.

counterevidence: Programme-affiliated evaluation, recall, broad fluid definition and contemporary changes prevent isolating a campaign effect.

episode.technology_configuration: A: research/camp oral rehydration delivery. B: home-prepared lobon-gur solution and packaged ORS supported by BRAC/community/distribution networks.
episode.task: Prevent or treat diarrhoeal dehydration; households could frame the task as stopping visible diarrhoea instead.
episode.population: A: defined clinical/camp populations in retrospective history. B: 90 sampled villages from three BRAC programme phases, not all Bangladesh.
episode.adoption_measure: B: recalled episodes in preceding two weeks; Table 2 broad ORT rates 51.8/54.5/53.0% with 1525/1114/1114 episodes; separate chemical testing of 269 preparations.
episode.observation_limits: Abstract 60% differs from all-episode table; discussion excludes dysentery. ORT includes other home fluids; no random assignment of teaching, exposure or products.

actors.chooser: Researchers and programme designers shaped delivery; caregivers selected responses, with medical and household advice.
actors.payer: NGO/government/donor programme resources; households supplied care time and sometimes purchased packets.
actors.operator_maintainer: Female teaching workers, monitors, retailers, medical staff and unpaid household caregivers.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Infants, children and ill adults dependent on others' recognition and care.
actors.ability_to_refuse: No compulsory household participation reported; illness, care dependency, money and availability constrained effective options. Research consent histories not established here.

labour.tasks: Paid teaching/monitoring and retail production/distribution complemented unpaid preparation and administration.
labour.entry_barriers: Teaching and preparation skills; product access and time; exact hiring barriers unexamined.
labour.bargaining_ownership: BRAC monitored teaching performance and linked pay to assessed learning; caregivers' bargaining and income effects unknown.
labour.transition: Decade-long teaching phases; no longitudinal employment/wage outcomes.
labour.distribution: Knowledge and reported use differentiated by episode/campaign cohort; not a livelihood distribution.
labour.evidence_limit: Cannot infer liberation of caregiver time or net professional displacement from a simple formulation.

title: Antibiotic prescribing and dispensing incentives in a Chinese city
summary: Randomized encounter scripts show an interaction between expressed demand and expected dispensing revenue; downstream harms were not measured.

stages.deployment: Established hospital dispensing/prescribing system studied, not invention of antibiotics.
stages.diffusion: No historical diffusion series; standardized encounters measure inappropriate use in a bounded population.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Lower prescribing under outside-pharmacy scripts provides a within-study negative comparison.
stages.displacement/reversal: Potential prescribing reduction, not demonstrated durable reform or discontinuation of needed treatment.

counterevidence: Scripts convey signals beyond money; young simulated patients in one city do not represent other conditions or real reform.

episode.technology_configuration: Hospital outpatient prescribing linked to expected medicine sales, tested with standardized mild-illness presentations.
episode.task: Authors evaluate appropriate prescribing; providers and patients may face different immediate objectives.
episode.population: Experiment 1: 320 visits to 80 physicians. Experiment 2: 300 visits to 120 physicians; young healthy auditors in one city.
contemporary_alternatives: No antibiotic prescription for study presentation
episode.adoption_measure: Antibiotic prescriptions per audited encounter; experiment 1 rates compare assigned scripts, not drug ingestion or national use.
episode.observation_limits: Auditors knew study goals; limited patient/city scope; no resistance or long-term policy measurement.

actors.chooser: Physicians prescribed; auditors manipulated demand and expected purchase location; hospital finance shaped context.
actors.payer: Patients ordinarily pay or use insurance; these audits record prescribed expenditure, not full system costs.
actors.operator_maintainer: Physicians, hospital/outside pharmacy staff; no production change investigated.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Patients bearing unnecessary expenditure/exposure; wider resistance costs are plausible but not observed here.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Auditors could request outside purchase; real patients' ability to choose depends on access and information. No universal freedom or coercion claim.

labour.tasks: Prescribing and dispensing tasks allocated across hospital and outside pharmacies; quality may change with revenue incentives.
labour.entry_barriers: Medical authority and dispensing infrastructure; entry/credential history not researched.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Hospitals and compensation arrangements connect revenue to practitioner incentives; no causal wage-distribution estimate.
labour.transition: Short audit observations only; no individual job transition or reform follow-up.
labour.distribution: Young standardized patients only; no distribution by age, income, morbidity or clinician livelihood.
labour.evidence_limit: Inappropriate prescribing response cannot be converted into net employment or physician-welfare effects.
